q: Which statement about values in Python is correct?
options: Every expression reduces to a value, and its data type decides what can be done with it
Only numbers count as values, while text is handled by a separate mechanism in the language
The operator alone decides what type a value has, whatever the value is at that point
Data types matter only when a value is printed, and never when values are combined
why: Every expression reduces to a value, and the type of that value decides which operations make sense for it.

q: Which three data types does chapter 1 work with?
options: Integers, lists and dictionaries
Strings, tuples and booleans
Integers, floating-point numbers and strings
Floats, sets and functions
why: The chapter works with integers, floating-point numbers and strings as its first three data types.

q: How does Python store integers and floating-point numbers?
options: Both exactly, the float just has a decimal point
Both in binary with the same fixed precision
Integers exactly, floats in binary with a fixed precision
Floats exactly, integers as approximate binary values
why: The two look alike in the shell but are stored differently: integers exactly, floats in binary with fixed precision.

q: What is special about a Python integer compared with integers in many other languages?
options: It is limited to 64 bits and wraps around silently when it gets too big
It has unlimited precision, so a huge result stays exact instead of overflowing
It is stored in binary, so large values are rounded to the nearest float
It can only hold values that fit in one machine word, or Python stops
why: A Python integer has unlimited precision, so a very large result is still exact and does not overflow.

q: What does this program print?
options: OverflowError
why: An integer has unlimited precision, so 2 ** 64 is exact and adding 1 keeps every digit.

q: Why is round(0.1 + 0.2, 2) used when a program wants to show 0.3?
options: Python cannot add two decimals exactly, so round does the addition instead of the plus sign
The raw float sum is a binary approximation slightly above 0.3, and round tidies it
The sum is exact, and round only changes how it prints
Floats are stored as text, and round converts the text to a number
why: Floats are stored in binary, so 0.1 + 0.2 is only close to 0.3 and rounding gives the clean value.

q: What does this program print?
options: True True
True False
False True
False False
why: The raw sum is 0.30000000000000004 and so is not equal to 0.3, but after round(..., 2) it is 0.3.

q: A shop program adds prices 0.1 and 0.2 and then tests the sum == 0.3, and the test fails. What is the best explanation?
options: The sum is stored in binary and is not exactly 0.3, so compare a rounded value
Python has a bug in the addition of decimals that only newer releases have fixed
Prices must always be integers, because floats cannot be added together in Python
The == operator is only allowed between strings and integers, never between floats
why: Some decimal fractions have no exact binary form, so the float sum is slightly off, and rounding before comparing avoids the problem.

q: How does chapter 1 treat text compared with numbers?
options: As a value like any other, handled with the same expression rules
As a special case that needs its own kind of statement
As a number in disguise that is stored as its digits
As something that can be printed but never combined
why: Text is a value like any other, and the chapter uses the same expression rules for it as for numbers.

q: What is a string in Python?
options: A whole number written without a decimal point
A number that has a fractional part
A name that stores a value in memory
A sequence of characters written between quotes
why: A string is a sequence of characters between quotes.

q: What does this program print?
options: ababc
ab2c
abbc
abcabc
why: The same operators act on strings with a different meaning: * repeats 'ab' twice and + then joins 'c' to the end.

q: Who decides which operator applies first in an expression?
options: The reader, by the way the expression is spaced
The operator that was typed first, from left to right
The data type of the last value in the expression
The language does, through fixed rules
why: The rules for which operator applies first are fixed by the language, not by the reader.

q: Which list is exactly the seven arithmetic operators of chapter 1?
why: The seven operators are +, -, *, /, //, % and **, evaluated in a documented order.

q: What is the difference between / and // in Python?
options: / divides numbers and // divides strings instead of numbers
/ gives a float quotient, while // gives the whole-number part of the division
// gives the remainder of the division and / gives the whole part
They give the same value, but // prints it without a decimal point
why: Floor division // keeps the whole-number quotient, while / gives the float result of the division.

q: Which order of operators is correct, from the one that binds first to the one that binds last?
options: ** first, then *, /, // and %, then + and -
*, /, // and % first, then **, then + and -
+ and - first, then *, /, // and %, then **
All operators together, from left to right
why: Precedence binds ** first, then *, /, // and %, then + and -, and parentheses override it.

q: What does this program print?
why: Without parentheses 2 ** 2 is 4, 4 * 4 is 16 and 10 - 16 is -6; with parentheses 10 - 4 is 6 and 6 * 4 is 24.

q: Which change makes the expression 8 - 2 * 3 evaluate to 18?
options: Write 8 - (2 * 3), because the product must come first
Write (8 - 2) * 3, because parentheses override the order
Write 8 - 2 * 3 with spaces around the operators
Write 8 - 2 ** 3, because ** binds first
why: Multiplication normally binds before subtraction giving 2, and only parentheses around 8 - 2 override the order to give 6 * 3.

q: What do 23 // 7 and 23 % 7 give together?
options: The whole part 3 and the remainder 2 of the division
The remainder 3 and the whole part 2 of the division
The rounded quotient 3 and the exact quotient 3.28
The float 3.2857 and the integer 23
why: Floor division gives the whole-number quotient and the modulus operator gives the remainder.

q: What does this program print?
why: // gives the whole quotient 3, % gives the remainder 2, and / gives the float 3.2857142857142856.

q: A program must split 47 minutes into whole hours and leftover minutes. Which pair of expressions does it?
options: 47 // 60 for the hours and 47 % 60 for the minutes
47 % 60 for the hours and 47 // 60 for the minutes
47 / 60 for the hours and 47 // 60 for the minutes
47 // 60 for both the hours and the minutes
why: Floor division gives the whole hours, which is 0 here, and the modulus operator gives the leftover 47 minutes.

q: Which two operators work on strings in chapter 1, and what do they do?
options: + repeats a string and * joins two strings
- removes text and / splits text
+ joins two strings and * repeats a string
+ and * both join strings, but * puts a space between them
why: Concatenation joins strings with + and replication repeats a string with *.

q: Why does joining a string to a number with + raise a TypeError?
options: Numbers can never appear in a program that also has strings in it
Python converts the string to a number and then finds that it is not one
The + operator only works on values that have exactly the same length
Python does not convert types silently, so the number must be converted first
why: Python does not convert types silently, so a string and a number cannot be joined until you write str() around the number.

q: What does this program print?
options: TypeError
Alice42
Alice 42
why: Joining a string to a number raises a TypeError because Python does not convert types silently; the except branch prints the class name.

q: Which fix makes 'Total: ' + 3 * 5 work and show Total: 15?
options: str('Total: ' + 3 * 5)
'Total: ' * 3 + 5
'Total: ' + str(3 * 5)
why: 3 * 5 is the integer 15, which must be converted to text before + can join it; wrapping the finished join in str() is too late.

q: What kind of value can be on the right of * when a string is on the left?
options: Another string, which is put after every character
A float, which is rounded to the nearest whole number
Any value, which is first converted to text
An integer, which is the number of repeats
why: Replication repeats a string an integer number of times with *.

q: What does this program print?
options: abab
ababab
ab2.0
TypeError
why: Replication needs an integer count, and 2.0 is a float, so the operation raises a TypeError.

q: What does a binding operation do?
options: It joins two values into one longer value
It converts a value from one type to another
It gives a value a name, so later expressions can use it
It prints a value on the screen
why: Assignment is the operation that gives a value a name so that later expressions can use it.

q: Which statement stores the value 42 in a variable called spam?
options: 42 = spam
spam == 42
spam = 42
store spam 42
why: An assignment statement stores a value in a variable with the = operator, with the name on the left.

q: Which variable name follows the PEP 8 recommendation?
options: TotalPrice
total_price
total-price
TOTAL PRICE
why: PEP 8 recommends lower_case names with underscores for variables.

q: What does this program print?
options: spam + 2
why: The variable is first bound to 40, and the second assignment stores the new value 40 + 2 under the same name.

q: Which six built-in functions does the first program of chapter 1 use?
options: print, input, len, list, int and float
print, open, len, str, int and float
print, input, sum, str, int and round
print, input, len, str, int and float
why: The chapter's six are print, input, len, str, int and float, all available without importing anything.

q: What does it mean that print and len are built-in functions?
options: They must be imported from a module before every use
They are always available, without importing anything
They are only available in the interactive shell
They can only be used inside a function you write
why: Built-in functions are always available in Python without an import.

q: Which pair of functions connects a program to its user?
options: input sends text out and print reads text in
len sends text out and str reads text in
print sends text out and input reads text in
print and input both send text out
why: print sends text out to the user and input reads text in from the user.

q: What does print() do with the value it is given?
options: It stores the value in a variable
It returns the value as a string to the program
It writes the value as text to the screen
It converts the value into an integer
why: print() writes its arguments as text to the screen.

q: What does this program print?
options: Hi 3 + 4
Hi7
Hi 7
Hi 34

q: What type of value does input() always return?
options: An integer
A float
Whatever type the user typed
A string
why: input() waits for the user to type and always returns a string.

q: A program runs age = input() and then print(age + 1). The user types 41. What happens?
options: A TypeError, because age is the text '41' and 1 is a number
It prints 42, because input() sees that 41 is a number
It prints 411, because + joins the digits
It prints 41, because the +1 is ignored
why: input() always returns a string, so age is '41' and joining a string to a number raises a TypeError.

q: Why do programs need str, int and float so often?
options: Because Python forgets the type of a value after every line
Because input returns text, and values must be converted to the type needed
Because numbers cannot be stored in variables without them
Because print refuses to write integers and floats
why: Since input gives text, programs convert values between types with str, int and float.

q: Why does int('4.2') fail?
options: The text is not a whole number, and int() refuses it with a ValueError
int() rounds 4.2 down to 4 but prints a warning message first
int() can only be used on values that are already numbers in the program
Text with a decimal point is always read as a float and then ignored
why: int() refuses a string that is not a whole number, and it does so with a ValueError.

q: What does this program print?
why: int() turns the texts into numbers so + adds them to 15, while the plain strings are joined into '78'.

q: What does this program print?
options: ValueError
TypeError
why: The text '4.2' is not a whole number, so int() raises a ValueError.

q: Which call turns the number 29 into the text '29'?
options: int(29)
float(29)
len(29)
str(29)
why: str() converts a value to a string, so str(29) gives '29'.

q: How is a measurement function such as len different from a conversion function?
options: It changes the value into a number and hides the original value
It only works on numbers and never on text values in a program
It writes the value on the screen instead of returning it
It reports a property of a value instead of changing its type
why: Measurement functions measure a value rather than convert it, and len is the first the chapter uses.

q: What does len() return for a string?
options: The number of words in it
The value of its last character
The number of characters in it
The number of characters minus one
why: The len function returns the number of characters in a string.

q: What does this program print?
why: len counts every character, including the space, so 'hello world' has 11, and the empty string has 0.

q: Why does the chapter say where code runs matters as much as what it says?
options: Because the same code always gives different answers on every computer you use
Because the Python students run in 2026 is newer than the one the chapter describes
Because Python code cannot run anywhere outside of the interactive shell
Because newer versions delete the built-in functions that older ones had
why: The Python students run is newer than the one the chapter describes, so the environment shapes what they see.

q: Which release is current in the chapter, and which one arrives on 1 October 2026?
options: 3.13 is current and 3.14 arrives
3.15 is current and 3.16 arrives
3.14 is current and 3.15 arrives
3.14 is current and 4.0 arrives

q: How does the interactive environment evaluate what you type?
options: All expressions wait and run together when you close the shell
Each expression is evaluated as soon as it is entered
Only statements run, and expressions must be printed first
Expressions run only after they have been saved in a file

Python 3.11
Python 3.12
Python 3.15

Only the print function can be used in it
It accepts strings but no longer accepts numbers

q: Why does the build of CPython matter to a programmer?
options: The build decides which operators the language has
The build decides how programs can use the machine
The build changes the meaning of every data type
The build is chosen by the program at run time
why: CPython is built in more than one way, and the build decides how programs can use the machine.

q: Since which release does CPython offer a free-threaded build, which was at first marked experimental?
options: Python 3.10
Python 3.12
Python 3.14
Python 3.13

q: Why is the free-threaded build in a chapter about basic expressions?
options: It speeds up integer arithmetic in every ordinary program that you write
It replaces the interactive shell that was used before Python 3.13
It previews the course's multithreading outcome, as it can run threads in parallel
It is needed to run any program that uses strings or numbers at all
why: The build can run threads in parallel, so it previews the course's multithreading outcome.

q: Why does an advanced course teach modern practice next to the book's basics?
options: Because the book's basics no longer work in current versions of Python
Because modern practice replaces the basics of the book completely
So the book's string building and first program are paired with today's tools
Because the basics are only meant for beginners and are skipped here
why: An advanced course teaches the current idiom alongside the book's basics.

q: Which statement about building strings is correct?
options: Concatenation works, but an f-string lets an expression sit between braces inside the string
Concatenation is deprecated and raises an error in newer versions of Python, so f-strings must be used
F-strings can only hold plain text, and they can never hold any values or any expressions at all
Mixing text and values is only possible with the input function of Python and with nothing else

options: It is evaluated while the string is built
It is kept as text, braces included
It is only allowed to be a variable name
It is evaluated before the whole program starts

options: PEP 8
PEP 701
PEP 20
PEP 3101

q: Where does a Python programmer's tool work start, according to the chapter?
options: With how the source code of a program is printed
With how packages and interpreters are installed
With how two strings are joined into one
With how the variables of a program are named
why: A Python programmer works through tools, starting with how packages and interpreters are installed.

options: It formats strings in the interactive shell
It installs Python packages and interpreters
It converts strings to integers
It measures the length of a program

It is a built-in function that is always available in every Python program

q: What do the data type and the expression have to do with each other?
options: A data type is a statement that stores a value in memory, and an expression is a kind of variable name
Every value has a data type, and an expression is code that evaluates to a value of some type
Only strings have a data type, and an expression is always a piece of text between quotes
The operator alone chooses the type of every value, so a value itself carries no type at all
why: The value model pairs two ideas: every value has a data type, and an expression is the piece of code that evaluates to a value.

q: In 7 + 1 and '7' + 1, what decides that the second one fails with a TypeError?
options: The second one has quotes around the digit, and quotes make Python skip every addition in the line
The second one uses a different operator from the first one, and that operator is not allowed
The first adds two integers, while the second asks + to combine a string and an integer
The number 7 cannot be used twice in the same program, so the second line is refused outright
why: The types of the operands decide what + can do: two integers are added, but a string and an integer do not combine without conversion.

q: Which function reports the data type of a value?
options: len
print
round
type
why: The type function reports the type of a value, for example <class 'int'> for 7.

q: Why does '7' + 1 raise a TypeError although 7 + 1 gives 8?
options: A string and an integer are different types, and + does not combine them without a conversion
The quotes turn the 7 into a floating-point number, and floats cannot be added to integers at all
The + operator only works on the digits from 0 to 9 and refuses anything written between quotes
Python can add values only after both of them have been stored in a variable of the same name
why: The type decides which operations are meaningful, so adding a string to an integer is refused instead of guessed.

q: What does this program print?
options: <class 'int'>
<class 'float'>
<class 'str'>
why: type(3.5) reports the type of a number with a fractional part, which is float.

q: Which of these is an expression?
options: spam = 42
while True:
import random

q: What does this program print?
why: The parentheses are evaluated first: 2 + 4 is 6, and 3 * 6 is 18.

q: In the expression 7 % 3, which part is the operator?
options: The symbol %
The number 7
The number 3
The whole expression
why: The symbol % is the operator; the numbers 7 and 3 are its operands.

q: Why can the symbol + both add numbers and join strings?
options: Python reads the symbol twice and tries the addition first
The type of the operands decides what the operator does
Strings are secretly stored as numbers, so + always adds
The symbol + is a function that the user has to define first
why: The same operator symbol can mean different things for different types: 2 + 3 adds, while 'a' + 'b' joins.

q: What does this program print?
why: 7 % 3 is the remainder 1, and 7 // 3 is the whole-number quotient 2.

q: In round(3.14159, 2), what are 3.14159 and 2 called?
options: Operators
Variables
Return values
Arguments
why: The values written inside the parentheses of a call are its arguments.

q: What is the value of the call len('hello')?
options: The function's return value, which is 5
The text hello, because len returns its argument
None, because len only prints a number
The function itself, because a call names it
why: A call evaluates to the value the function returns; len returns the number of characters.

q: What does this program print?
why: round with a second argument of 3 keeps three decimals: 2.71828 becomes 2.718.

q: What does calling a function mean?
options: Writing the function's name in a comment so that the code is documented for later readers
Storing the function in a variable without running it, so that it can be run some other time
Asking Python to run the function now, with the given arguments
Deleting the function from the program after its first use, so that it cannot run again
why: Calling a function means asking Python to run it now, with the values written in the parentheses.

q: Why does a program that contains only the word print on a line display nothing?
options: The word print only works inside the interactive shell, and a saved program skips it
Python skips every line that holds a single word, so the line is read and then ignored
The function needs a variable to be assigned to it first, and the program has no such variable
Without parentheses the line names the function and does not call it
why: The parentheses make the call; without them the name only refers to the function.

q: After spam = 42, what is spam?
options: A name that refers to the value 42
A function that returns 42
A string that holds the characters 42
A comment about the number 42
why: A variable is a name that refers to a value.

q: What happens when a program reads a name that was never assigned?
options: Python gives the name the value 0
Python raises a NameError
Python returns None and continues
Python creates the variable as an empty string
why: A name that was never assigned cannot be used; reading it raises a NameError.

q: Which variable name follows the PEP 8 recommendation?
options: MyAge
my age
my_age
MY-AGE
why: PEP 8 recommends lowercase words separated by underscores; a space or a minus sign cannot be part of a name.

q: What is the difference between the Python language and a Python implementation?
options: The language is the interactive shell, and an implementation is a saved file with a name
They are two names for the same thing and never differ in any way, so the question is moot
The implementation defines the grammar and the meaning, and the language is only a tool that runs it
The language defines what a program means, and an implementation is a program that carries it out
why: The language defines what a program means; the implementation decides how the computer does it.

q: Which Python implementation does this course use?
options: CPython
Jython
IronPython
TypeScript
why: The course uses CPython; Jython and IronPython are other implementations of the language.

q: What does the Python interpreter do?
options: It translates Python code into Java before anyone runs it
It reads Python code and runs it
It only checks the spelling of a program and never runs it
It stores the packages that a project needs
why: The interpreter is the program that reads Python code and runs it.

q: Why does the Python glossary say that the difference between interpreted and compiled can be blurry for Python?
options: Python programs must always be compiled to an executable before use
Python code is typed into a compiler by hand
Source code is first compiled to bytecode by the bytecode compiler
The interpreter can only run a program that is compiled twice
why: Python is called interpreted, but source code is compiled to bytecode before the virtual machine runs it.

q: What happens when the python command is run with no arguments?
options: The last saved script is run
The interpreter exits at once with an error
A virtual environment is created
The interactive shell starts
why: With no arguments the interpreter opens the interactive shell; with a file name it runs the script.

q: What is CPython?
options: The canonical implementation of Python, as distributed on python.org
A separate language that is almost the same as Python but is meant for web pages
A library of packages for numerical work that every Python program must import first
A tool that installs packages from the internet into the folder of the current project
why: CPython is the canonical implementation of the Python programming language, as distributed on python.org.

q: Why is the name CPython needed?
options: To name the version of the language that comes after Python 3 in the release schedule
To tell this implementation apart from others such as Jython or IronPython
To mark code that is written in the C language only and cannot be read by a learner
To separate Python programs from programs that are written for the web in other languages
why: The term CPython is used when it is necessary to distinguish this implementation from other implementations.

q: In the standard Python from python.org, what does sys.implementation.name hold?
options: 'python'
'jython'
'cpython'
'ironpython'
why: sys.implementation.name names the implementation that is running, which is 'cpython' here.

q: What is bytecode?
options: The text of a program exactly as the student typed it, kept in the file that is run
A file format for images that Python can print on the screen when a program asks
A secret key that protects a program from being copied by other people on the machine
The internal representation of a program inside CPython, produced by compiling the source code
why: Python source code is compiled into bytecode, which a virtual machine executes.

q: Why should a program never depend on bytecode instructions?
options: They are not expected to be stable between Python releases or to work on other virtual machines
They can be read only by the user who wrote the program and by nobody else on the machine
They are deleted from memory after the first line of the program has been run once
They are different on every line of the same program, so no two lines can share them
why: Bytecodes are an implementation detail of CPython and its version.

q: How can a user tell which build of CPython is running?
options: By counting the lines of the program that is run and comparing the count with a table
From the output of python -VV or by calling sys._is_gil_enabled()
By checking whether the program contains a print call near the top of the file
By reading the name of the folder that holds the program, which always names the build
why: The output of python -VV names a free-threaded build, and sys._is_gil_enabled() tells whether the GIL is on in the running process.

q: What is a thread?
options: A string that is repeated several times
A variable that cannot be changed
A separate flow of execution inside one program
A package that is installed from the internet
why: A thread is a separate flow of execution, so several activities can be in progress inside one program.

q: What do all the threads of one program share?
options: A private copy of every variable, made when each thread starts
One processor core that no other program may use at the same time
The same line of the source code at every moment of the run
The same memory space
why: The threading module operates within a single process, so all threads share the same memory.

q: What does the global interpreter lock ensure?
options: Only one thread executes Python bytecode at a time
Every thread gets a core of its own
Strings can never be changed by a program
The program runs once and then stops
why: The GIL is the mechanism CPython uses so that only one thread executes Python bytecode at a time.

q: Why does the GIL limit what threads gain on heavy calculations?
options: It slows down the keyboard of the user, so that the program receives less input per second
Only one thread can run Python bytecode at a time, so the cores of a multi-core machine are not used in parallel
It turns every calculation into a string operation, which takes longer than the original
It stops the whole program after the first thread has finished, so the others never start
why: Locking the entire interpreter loses much of the parallelism that multi-processor machines offer.

q: Why is the GIL less of a problem for a program that mostly waits for input and output?
options: Input and output run in a different language, so the lock never applies to the waiting lines of code
Waiting threads are deleted from the program as soon as they start waiting, so they cannot block
The GIL is released when the program does input and output
The GIL is switched on only while the program does arithmetic, and it is off for every other task
why: The GIL is always released when doing I/O, so waiting threads do not block the others.

q: Which configuration option builds a free-threaded CPython?
options: --enable-threads
--no-bytecode
--free-memory
--disable-gil
why: A free-threaded build is configured with the --disable-gil option before compilation.

q: Which items belong to the documented schedule of a Python release?
options: A first release date, a period of bug fixes, a period of security fixes and an end-of-life date
A list of the students who may use it and the date of the exam that they will sit later
A price, a licence key and a renewal date, as for a product that is sold in a shop
Only a first release date, because a release is never retired once it has been published
why: Each release has a first release, a bugfix period, a security period and an end-of-life date.

q: In sys.version_info for Python 3.14.4, what are the three numbers called?
options: year, month and day
major, minor and micro
language, library and tool
build, branch and tag
why: sys.version_info has the fields major, minor and micro: 3, 14 and 4 here.

q: Which release made free-threaded Python officially supported?
options: Python 3.12
Python 3.13
Python 3.14
Python 3.15
why: Python 3.13 added the free-threaded build as experimental, and Python 3.14 made it officially supported.

q: Why does a learner need to know which Python version is in use?
options: The version decides how many lines a program may have
The version is needed to log in to the interactive shell
The version only matters for programs that print text
The version decides which features a program can use
why: Features such as the new interactive interpreter appeared in a particular release, so a newer program may fail on an older one.

q: What does PEP stand for?
options: Python Enhancement Proposal
Python Execution Policy
Program Error Protocol
Package Extension Plan
why: A PEP is a Python Enhancement Proposal, a design document for the Python community.

q: What is a PEP used for?
options: To store the packages that a project installs, so that they can be found by later projects
To propose major new features, collect community input and document design decisions
To run a program on several cores at once, without any change to the source code
To check the spelling of a program before it is saved to the disk of the computer
why: PEPs are the primary mechanism for proposing features, collecting input and documenting design decisions.

q: Which PEP is the style guide for Python code?
options: PEP 1
PEP 701
PEP 8
PEP 703
why: PEP 8 is the Style Guide for Python Code; PEP 1 describes PEPs, PEP 701 formalised f-strings and PEP 703 made the GIL optional.

q: What is a package in Python?
options: A string that holds several lines of text, written between three quotation marks in a row
A function that is always available without importing anything, like len and print
A comment that groups several lines of code together so that a reader can skip them
A module that can contain submodules
why: A package is a Python module that can contain submodules or subpackages.

q: Why can one Python installation not satisfy every application?
options: Application A may need version 1.0 of a module while application B needs version 2.0
Every application needs its own copy of the interactive shell
Only one program may be written per installation
Packages can be installed only once per day
why: If two applications need conflicting versions of a module, installing either version leaves the other unable to run.

q: What is a virtual environment?
options: A program that pretends to be another computer so that code can be tried on it safely
A self-contained directory tree with a Python installation and additional packages
A list of the functions that Python provides, kept in a file in the project folder
A window in which the interactive shell is shown, with the colours of the current theme
why: A virtual environment is a self-contained directory tree that contains a Python installation plus a number of packages.

q: Which command creates a virtual environment in a directory named tutorial-env?
options: python -m pip tutorial-env
python -c venv.run
python -m venv tutorial-env
python -m env tutorial-env
why: The venv module is run as a script with the directory path: python -m venv tutorial-env.

q: What problem does a virtual environment solve?
options: It makes a program run faster on every computer, whatever the programs inside it are doing
It removes the need to write any code, because the environment can write it for the user
It lets two programs share a single variable, so that they can both read and change it
Different applications can use different versions of the same package without affecting each other
why: Application A can keep version 1.0 while application B uses version 2.0, and upgrading one does not affect the other.

q: What does a package manager do?
options: It installs, upgrades and removes packages and tracks the versions a project needs
It checks that every variable in a project has a lowercase name and reports those that do not
It translates a program into another language so that it can be read by a colleague abroad
It prints the output of a program on paper whenever the program ends with an error message
why: A package manager keeps track of the packages and versions a project needs; uv is one for Python.
